title: Is a pane a cell grid with pixel regions, or free pixels?
body:
Nothing in the code defines a pane yet. The project rule is that the UI
pretends it has a TUI's limits, and uses pixels only where nothing else would
do. That rule is the main input to this decision.

A pane program produces output the host shows. What that output is made of
decides the protocol's vocabulary, what the host renderer has to draw, and
how an existing terminal program becomes a pane.

## Options

| Option | What a pane sends | What the host draws | Existing TUI tools |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cell grid with pixel regions | Cells with attributes, plus a pixel region anchored to a cell rectangle | One glyph atlas pass and one texture pass | Work unchanged |
| Free pixels | A surface the pane renders into, as a Wayland client does | Composites surfaces | Need a terminal pane wrapped around them |
| Scene description | Text runs, rectangles, paths, images, in pane coordinates | A small 2D renderer | Need a terminal pane that converts cells to a scene |

Cell grid with pixel regions. The cell is the unit of layout, input and
scrolling. A pixel region is a rectangle of cells that a pane paints with
image data, in the way kitty's graphics protocol places an image over cells.
Highlighting lines of code, drawing a box around a block, and showing three
files side by side are all cell operations. A diagram is a pixel region.
The host needs one renderer, and it is the renderer every terminal emulator
already has.

Free pixels. Any language and any toolkit can be a pane, and the host is a
compositor. The cost is that the host knows nothing about what is in a pane,
so "highlight lines 40 to 60" has to be reinvented by every pane program with
its own channel and its own meaning. The TUI rule would be a convention
rather than something the protocol enforces.

Scene description. The pane sends shapes and text runs and the host draws
them. Richer than cells, poorer than pixels, and it needs a renderer the host
would otherwise not have. The TUI rule makes most of that richness
unavailable, so the extra cost buys little.

## Lean

Cell grid with pixel regions. It is the only option where the TUI rule is a
property of the protocol rather than a request to pane authors, and the only
one where a terminal program is already a pane.

## Cost

- The pixel region needs rules for scrolling, resizing and overlap. kitty's
  answers are a starting point: anchor to a cell, clip to the region, drop on
  scroll unless the pane says otherwise.
- The host cannot show anything a cell grid cannot express, by design.

## Open

- Whether a pane can declare a region as "cells only" so the host can
  guarantee it never needs the texture pass for ordinary panes.
- The cell attribute set: colours, weight, underline styles, and whether
  a cell can carry an opaque id that the agent channel can refer to.
close_reason: Resolved on 2026-11-06 by making decade a nested Wayland compositor. An app pane is the client's own buffer, which is the free-pixels option, and only decade's chrome and native panes are a cell grid. No pixel-region protocol of decade's own is needed, since Wayland is the pixel channel. The cell-grid code stays for the chrome. The milestone decade-71e626 carries the full description.
